code.originalText: Endocrinology consultation with a cosyntropin stimulation test, diagnosis, and start of replacement

text.paragraph: Three-day review, seen the same morning by endocrinology for a cosyntropin stimulation test. [S]

Ms. Austen returns three days after her first visit and was seen this morning by Dr. Varga-Whitlock of endocrinology, who performed a cosyntropin stimulation test. Since her last visit she has salted her food freely and has felt about the same: tired, with little appetite, a bout of nausea each morning, and lightheadedness when she stands quickly. She vomited once two days ago but kept fluids down afterwards. She has had no fainting, confusion, or severe abdominal pain. Her back still aches by the end of the day. She has brought a page of notes on how she has felt each day since the winter. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1816-03-19; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Thin and tired but alert; weight 51.8 kg
100/64 lying, pulse 88; 86/56 after three minutes standing, pulse 106: a postural drop of 14 mmHg systolic

Diffuse bronze darkening of the face and the backs of the hands, deeper in the palmar creases, knuckles and an old scar on the forearm, with patches of brown pigment on the gums and inside the cheeks; pale lips
No cervical, supraclavicular, axillary or inguinal nodes
Soft and non-tender; no enlarged liver or spleen

About three months of increasing tiredness, loss of 5 kg, darkening of the skin, nausea with bouts of vomiting, low back ache, salt craving and lightheadedness on standing, with low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils; adrenal insufficiency suspected and urgent endocrinology testing booked
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the diagnosis at the consultation; its timing echoes the documented break in her health (D).

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease): no cortisol response to cosyntropin with a markedly raised ACTH, and mineralocorticoid deficiency with raised renin and low aldosterone; on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; synthetic modern diagnosis chosen for a historical illness whose cause is disputed
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; the historical cause of her illness remains undetermined (R, disputed).
Mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL) with normal ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate
S — Synthetic finding at intake; it recovers on replacement.

list.item:
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) (E27.1). The 8 am cortisol is 2.6 ug/dL with an ACTH of 548 pg/mL, and cortisol does not rise after cosyntropin (3.4 ug/dL at 30 minutes and 3.9 ug/dL at 60 minutes, far below 18): primary adrenal insufficiency is confirmed. Plasma renin activity 16.2 ng/mL/h with aldosterone 1.8 ng/dL shows mineralocorticoid deficiency as well, which explains the low sodium, high potassium and postural drop. The cause is not yet known; autoimmune adrenalitis is by far the commonest, and tuberculosis and infiltration (including lymphoma) are the others to exclude. Dr. Varga-Whitlock and I agree to start treatment today. [S]
Hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg at 2 pm, first doses taken in clinic.
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg each morning.
Emergency hydrocortisone injection kit with training, written sick-day rules, a steroid emergency card, and a medical ID.
21-hydroxylase antibodies, A1c and celiac serology at the two-week visit.
Electrolytes in two weeks; renin at six weeks.

Mild normocytic anemia (D64.9). Hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL with a normal MCV, ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate at the first visit: the pattern seen in untreated adrenal insufficiency, expected to recover on replacement. [S]
Repeat the blood count at the two- and six-week visits.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia monograph (2026); American College of Gastroenterology Guidelines Update: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease (2023)

Follow-up: Two-week visit with electrolytes, blood count, 21-hydroxylase antibodies, A1c and celiac serology. Inject and call 911 for vomiting, fainting or confusion; follow the sick-day rules for any fever. Next scheduled visit 1816-04-02: two-week review after starting replacement: electrolytes, cause, and autoimmune screening. [S]
